question: Which statement best describes The call stack?
options: JavaScript executes one thing at a time on a single call stack — a LIFO structure that tracks which function is currently running and who called it. When you call a function it is pushed; when it returns it is popped. While the stack is non-empty, nothing else (no timer, no promise callback) can run, which is why long synchronous work blocks the entire page.

When a Web API finishes (a timer fires, a click happens, a network response arrives), its callback is placed on the task queue — also called the macrotask or callback queue. The event loop takes ONE task from this queue per loop tick, but only after the call stack is empty and all microtasks have drained.

Async-capable operations like setTimeout, fetch, DOM events, and I/O are not part of the JavaScript language — they are provided by the host (the browser or Node). When you call them, JS hands the work off to the host and immediately continues. The host does the waiting on a separate thread and, when ready, queues a callback for the event loop to pick up later.

Promise reactions (.then/.catch/.finally callbacks), queueMicrotask, and async/await continuations go on a separate, higher-priority microtask queue. After each task finishes and before the next render or next task, the event loop drains the ENTIRE microtask queue. This is why promise callbacks always run before setTimeout callbacks.

question: Which statement best describes The task (callback / macrotask) queue?
options: setTimeout(fn, 0) does NOT run fn immediately or even synchronously. It tells the host to enqueue fn as a task after at least 0ms. Because the current synchronous code must finish (emptying the stack) and all microtasks must drain first, fn is delayed until a future loop tick — often noticeably later than promise callbacks scheduled afterward.

question: Which statement best describes The loop itself?
options: Because the loop drains ALL microtasks before doing anything else, a microtask that keeps scheduling more microtasks can starve the event loop: timers never fire, the page never re-renders, and the UI freezes even though no single piece of code blocks. This is a subtle hazard of recursive promise chains or queueMicrotask loops.
